units.greek: πᾶσαι μὲν οὖν αὗται διὰ φανερῶν αἰτιῶν γίγνονται αἱ βλάβαι τῆς δυνάμεως· ἕτεραι δέ εἰσιν ἀφανεῖς, ὥσπερ ὅταν ἄνευ κενώσεως φανερᾶς ἢ ἀγρυπνίας ἢ λιμαγχονίας ἢ καὶ τῆς κατὰ τὸ στόμα κοιλίας αἰσθήσεως οἱ κάμνοντες εἰς τοιαύτην ὑποσύρωνται τοῦ σώματος διάθεσιν, οἵαν ἐν τῷ προγνωστικῷ κατὰ τὴν ἀρχὴν αὐτὸς ἔγραψε λέγων· ῥὶς ὀξεῖα, ὀφθαλμοὶ κοῖλοι, [608] κρόταφοι συμπεπτωκότες, ὅσα τε τούτων ἐφεξῆς. αὕτη γὰρ τοῦ σώματος ἡ κατάστασις γίνεται μὲν καὶ δι᾿ ἀγρυπνίαν καὶ δι᾿ ἔκκρισίν τινα πολλὴν καὶ λιμαγχονίαν· γίνεται δὲ καὶ χωρὶς τούτων, ὅταν οἵ τε ἐν τῷ σώματι χυμοὶ λεπτοὶ τυγχάνουσιν ὄντες ἥ τε τοῦ πυρετοῦ θερμασία δριμεῖα· διαφοροῦνται γὰρ οἱ οὕτως λεπτυνόμενοι κατὰ τὸ ἄδηλον. ἐνίοις δὲ καὶ κατὰ τὴν δυσκρασίαν μιᾶς τῶν ἀρχῶν παθούσης ἀσθενὴς ἡ δύναμις γίγνεται· πρώτη μὲν οὖν ἡ πρώτως παθοῦσα κάμνει, κατὰ συμπάθειαν δὲ καὶ αἱ λοιπαὶ δύο. μεμάθηκας γὰρ ἄλλην μὲν εἶναι κατὰ τὰ νεῦρα δύναμιν, ἀρχὴν ἔχουσαν τὸν ἐγκέφαλον· ἄλλην δὲ κατὰ τὰς ἀρτηρίας, ἧς ἡ ἀρχὴ καρδία· καὶ τρίτην κατὰ τὰς φλέβας, ἐξ ἥπατος ὁρμωμένην· ἐνίοτε γοῦν τῶν μορίων ἑνὸς οὑτινοσοῦν δυσκρασία τὴν οἰκείαν δύναμιν ἐκάκωσεν, ᾗ συνεπάθησαν αἱ λοιπαὶ δύο δυνάμεις. τάχισται μὲν οὖν ἀπώλειαι γίγνονται τῆς καρδίας παθούσης, ἐφεξῆς δὲ τοῦ ἐγκεφάλου, βραδεῖαι δὲ αἱ ἀπὸ τοῦ ἥπατος.

ὥσπερ γὰρ ταῦτα τὰ μόρια [609] κατὰ δυσκρασίαν παθόντα μεγίστην βλάβην βλάπτεται τῆς οἰκείας ἕκαστον δυνάμεως, οὕτως ἔνια πλησίον ἑκάστης ἀρχῆς κείμενα κατὰ δυσκρασίαν ἰσχυρῶς νοσήσαντα τὰς ἀρχὰς τῶν δυνάμεων εἰς συμπάθειαν ἑαυτοῖς ἄγει, τινὰ δὲ, κᾂν μὴ πλησίον ᾖ κείμενα, διὰ τὴν κατὰ γένος κοινωνίαν, ἤ τινα διαθέσεως ἰδιότητα, τὰ τὰς ἀρχὰς τῶν δυνάμεων ἔχοντα βλάπτει μόρια. τὸ μὲν οὖν στόμα τῆς γαστρὸς ὅταν μὲν ζωτικὴν δύναμιν εἰς συμπάθειαν ἄγῃ, συγκοπὰς ἐπιφέρει, ὅταν δὲ τὴν ἰδίως ψυχικὴν ὀνομαζομένην, παραφροσύνας ἢ σπασμούς· ἡ δὲ μήτρα ποτὲ μὲν ἀπνοίας, ποτὲ δὲ συντάσεις νεύρων. ἀλλὰ συμπληρωθέντα μὲν ἕκαστα τούτων ἁπλῶς γνώριμα, συνιστάμενα δὲ καὶ αὐξανόμενα κατὰ βραχὺ λανθάνει τοὺς πολλοὺς τῶν ἰατρῶν. χρὴ δὲ οὐχ ὅταν ὑπὸ μεγέθους ἀβοήθητα γένηται, τότε γνωρίζειν αὐτὰ τοῖς ἰδιώταις ὡσαύτως, ἀλλὰ ἀρχόμενά τε καὶ γιγνόμενα, τοῦτο γὰρ κάλλιστον· εἰ δὲ μὴ, ἀλλ᾿ αὐξανόμενά γε πάντως.

ἅπαντα οὖν τὰ τοιαῦτα δοκεῖ μοι δηλῶσαι διὰ τῆσδε τῆς λέξεως ὁ Ἱπποκράτης, ἐν ᾗ φησιν· ὅσα τε ἡμέων [610] ἡ φύσις καὶ ἕξις ἑκάστοισιν ἐκτεκνοῖ πάθεα καὶ εἴδεα παντοῖα· καὶ νῦν φύσιν λέγει τὴν κρᾶσιν, ἕξιν δὲ αὐτοῦ τοῦ σώματος τὴν κατασκευήν. οἱ μὲν γὰρ ἀραιότεροι φύσει διαφοροῦνται καὶ συγκόπτονται |ῥᾳδίως, οἱ δὲ πυκνότεροι χρονίζουσιν ἐν ταῖς νόσοις. οὕτω δὲ καὶ μόρια τὰ μὲν ἔχουσί τινες ψυχρότερα, τὰ δὲ θερμότερα, καὶ τὰ μὲν ξηρότερα, τὰ δὲ ὑγρότερα· ἅπασι δὲ οἰκεῖον τῇ κράσει τὸ νόσημα. Μεῖζον μὲν γὰρ κακόν ἐστιν, ἢν διὰ τὸν πόνον καὶ τὴν ὀξύτητα τῆς νούσου ἀσθενέοντι προσφέρῃ τις ποτὸν ἢ ῥόφημα πλεῖον ἢ σιτίον, οἰόμενος διὰ κενεαγγείην ἀσθενέειν. ἀεικὲς δὲ καὶ διὰ κενεαγγείην ἀσθενέοντα μὴ γνῶναι καὶ πιέζειν τῇ διαίτῃ. φέρει μὲν γάρ τινα κίνδυνον καὶ αὕτη ἡ ἁμαρτὰς, πολλῷ δὲ ἧσσον τῆς ἑτέρης· καταγελαστοτέρη δὲ πολλῷ αὕτη μᾶλλον ἡ ἁμαρτὰς τῆς ἑτέρης.

εἰ [611] γὰρ ἄλλος ἰητρὸς ἢ καὶ ἰδιώτης ἐσελθὼν καὶ γνοὺς τὰ ξυμβεβηκότα δώῃ καὶ φαγεῖν καὶ πιεῖν ἃ ὁ ἕτερος ἐκώλυσεν, ἐπιδήλως ἂν δοκέῃ ὠφεληκέναι. τὰ δὲ τοιάδε μάλιστα καθυβρίζεται τῶν χειρωνακτέων ὑπὸ τῶν ἀνθρώπων, δοκέει γὰρ αὐτέοισιν ὁ ἐσελθὼν ἰητρὸς ἢ ἰδιώτης ὥσπερ εἰ καὶ τεθνειότα ἀναστήσας. Διὰ τὰς ὀδύνας πολλάκις οἱ κάμνοντες ἄσφυκτοι γίγνονται καὶ λειποψυχοῦσι καὶ κίνησιν οὐδεμίαν οἷόν τε κινηθῆναι, κατὰ ταῦτα δὲ καὶ διὰ τὴν ὀξύτητα τῆς νόσου· τινὲς δὲ οὐ διὰ ταῦτα κάμνουσι τὴν δύναμιν, ἀλλὰ διὰ κένωσιν ἀγγείων ὁπωσοῦν γεγονυῖαν, εἴτ᾿ οὖν δι᾿ ἔκκρισιν πρόδηλον αἰσθήσει, εἴτε διαφόρησιν, εἴτε καὶ διὰ λιμαγχονίαν. οὗτοι μὲν οὖν δέονται τροφὴν προσάρασθαι ὅτι τάχιστα· τοὐναντίον δὲ ἂν οἱ δι᾿ ὀδύνην ἢ δι᾿ ὀξύτητα τῆς νόσου, κενώσεως ἐνίοτε χρῄζουσι μᾶλλον ἢ πληρώσεως.

ἀλλὰ τούτοις μὲν ὁ τροφὴν διδοὺς μέγιστόν τι κακὸν ἐργάζεται· τοὺς δὲ διὰ κενεαγγείην ἀσθενοῦντας εἰ πιέζει διαίτῃ λεπτῇ, [612] βλάψειεν, οὐχ ὁμοίως δὲ ἐπιφανῶς ἢ ὀξέως· ἀεικές γε μήν ἐστιν ἀγνοῆσαι τοὺς διὰ κένωσιν ἀσθενοῦντας μᾶλλον ἢ τοὺς δι᾿ ὀδύνην. τὰ δ᾿ ἄλλα τῆς ῥήσεως σαφῆ. Γεγράψεται οὖν καὶ περὶ τούτων σημήϊα, οἶσι δεῖ ἕκαστα τουτέων διαγινώσκειν. Ἐπαγγέλλεται οὖν πάλιν κᾀνταῦθα, ὥσπερ ὀλίγον ἔμπροσθεν, ἕτερόν τι γράψαι περὶ τῶν ὀξέων νοσημάτων βιβλίον. Παραπλήσια μέντοι τοῖσι κατὰ κοιλίην ἐστὶ καὶ ταῦτα. καὶ γὰρ ἢν ὅλον τὸ σῶμα ἀναπαύσηται πουλὺ παρὰ τὸ ἔθος, οὐκ αὐτίκα ἔῤῥωται μᾶλλον· ἢν δὲ δὴ καὶ πλείονα χρόνον διελινύσας ἐξαπίνης εἰς τοὺς πόνους ἔλθοι, φλαῦρόν τι πρήξειεν ἐπιδήλως. οὕτω δὲ καὶ ἓν ἕκαστον τοῦ σώματος.

term_table.english_sentence_A: All these injuries of the faculty, then, come about through manifest causes; but there are others that are non-manifest, as when, without any manifest evacuation or sleeplessness or starvation or even any sensation at the mouth of the belly, the patients are drawn down into such a condition of the body as he himself described at the beginning of the Prognostic, saying: 'nose sharp, eyes hollow, [608] temples collapsed,' and all that follows these.
term_table.english_sentence_B: All these, then, are the injuries to the faculty that come about through evident causes; but there are others that are non-evident, as when, without evident evacuation or sleeplessness or starvation, or even the sensation in the mouth of the stomach, the patients are drawn down into such a condition of the body as he himself wrote of at the beginning of the Prognostic, saying: 'nose sharp, eyes hollow, [608] temples fallen in', and whatever follows these.

term_table.greek_sentence: αὕτη γὰρ τοῦ σώματος ἡ κατάστασις γίνεται μὲν καὶ δι᾿ ἀγρυπνίαν καὶ δι᾿ ἔκκρισίν τινα πολλὴν καὶ λιμαγχονίαν· γίνεται δὲ καὶ χωρὶς τούτων, ὅταν οἵ τε ἐν τῷ σώματι χυμοὶ λεπτοὶ τυγχάνουσιν ὄντες ἥ τε τοῦ πυρετοῦ θερμασία δριμεῖα· διαφοροῦνται γὰρ οἱ οὕτως λεπτυνόμενοι κατὰ τὸ ἄδηλον.
term_table.english_sentence_A: For this state of the body comes about both through sleeplessness and through some copious excretion and starvation; but it also comes about apart from these, when the humours in the body happen to be thin and the heat of the fever acrid; for those thus attenuated are dispersed imperceptibly.
term_table.english_sentence_B: For this state of the body comes about both through sleeplessness and through some copious excretion and starvation; but it comes about also without these, when the humours in the body happen to be thin and the heat of the fever acrid; for those that are thus thinned are dissipated imperceptibly.

term_table.greek_sentence: ἐνίοις δὲ καὶ κατὰ τὴν δυσκρασίαν μιᾶς τῶν ἀρχῶν παθούσης ἀσθενὴς ἡ δύναμις γίγνεται· πρώτη μὲν οὖν ἡ πρώτως παθοῦσα κάμνει, κατὰ συμπάθειαν δὲ καὶ αἱ λοιπαὶ δύο.
term_table.english_sentence_A: In some people, too, the faculty becomes weak in consequence of a dyskrasia, when one of the principles has been affected; first, then, the one primarily affected suffers, and by sympathy the remaining two as well.
term_table.english_sentence_B: In some, too, the faculty becomes weak through the dyscrasia of one of the principles, when it is affected; first, then, the one primarily affected is distressed, and by sympathy the remaining two as well.

term_table.english_sentence_A: For you have learned that there is one faculty in the nerves, having the brain as its principle; another in the arteries, whose principle is the heart; and a third in the veins, proceeding from the liver. At any rate, sometimes a dyskrasia of any one whatsoever of the parts has damaged its proper faculty, and with it the remaining two faculties have suffered in sympathy.
term_table.english_sentence_B: For you have learned that there is one faculty in the nerves, having the brain as its principle; another in the arteries, whose principle is the heart; and a third in the veins, setting out from the liver. Sometimes, at any rate, a dyscrasia of any one of the parts whatsoever has damaged its own faculty, with which the remaining two faculties have been affected in sympathy.

term_table.english_sentence_A: Thus the mouth of the stomach, whenever it draws the vital faculty into sympathy, brings on syncopes, and whenever it draws in the faculty properly called psychic, deliriums or spasms; and the womb at one time brings on cessations of breathing, at another tensions of the nerves.

A.translation: All these injuries of the faculty, then, come about through manifest causes; but there are others that are non-manifest, as when, without any manifest evacuation or sleeplessness or starvation or even any sensation at the mouth of the belly, the patients are drawn down into such a condition of the body as he himself described at the beginning of the Prognostic, saying: 'nose sharp, eyes hollow, [608] temples collapsed,' and all that follows these. For this state of the body comes about both through sleeplessness and through some copious excretion and starvation; but it also comes about apart from these, when the humours in the body happen to be thin and the heat of the fever acrid; for those thus attenuated are dispersed imperceptibly. In some people, too, the faculty becomes weak in consequence of a dyskrasia, when one of the principles has been affected; first, then, the one primarily affected suffers, and by sympathy the remaining two as well. For you have learned that there is one faculty in the nerves, having the brain as its principle; another in the arteries, whose principle is the heart; and a third in the veins, proceeding from the liver. At any rate, sometimes a dyskrasia of any one whatsoever of the parts has damaged its proper faculty, and with it the remaining two faculties have suffered in sympathy. The swiftest destructions, then, occur when the heart is affected, next when the brain is, while those proceeding from the liver are slow.

For just as these parts, [609] when they are affected by dyskrasia, suffer the greatest harm, each in its own faculty, so some parts lying near each principle, when they fall severely ill through dyskrasia, draw the principles of the faculties into sympathy with themselves, while certain others, even if they do not lie nearby, by reason of their community of kind, or some peculiarity of their condition, harm the parts that contain the principles of the faculties. Thus the mouth of the stomach, whenever it draws the vital faculty into sympathy, brings on syncopes, and whenever it draws in the faculty properly called psychic, deliriums or spasms; and the womb at one time brings on cessations of breathing, at another tensions of the nerves. But each of these, once fully developed, is straightforwardly recognizable, whereas while they are forming and increasing little by little they escape the notice of most physicians. Yet one must recognize them not when through their magnitude they have become beyond help, in the same manner as laymen do, but when they are beginning and coming into being, for this is best; and if not, then at any rate certainly while they are increasing.

All such things, then, Hippocrates seems to me to have indicated through this phrase, in which he says: 'and all the affections and forms of every kind that our [610] nature and habit beget in each of us'; and here he calls the mixture 'nature', and the constitution of the body itself 'habit'. For those who are by nature more rarefied are easily dispersed and fall into syncope, whereas the denser ones linger long in their diseases. So too some people have certain parts colder, others hotter, and some drier, others moister; and in all cases the disease is akin to the mixture. For it is a greater evil if, on account of the pain and the acuteness of the disease, one administers to a person who is weak more drink or gruel or food, supposing that he is weak on account of emptiness of the vessels. But it is also unseemly not to recognize one who is weak on account of emptiness of the vessels and to press him hard with the regimen. For this error too carries some danger, but much less than the other; yet this error is far more ridiculous than the other.

For if [611] another physician, or even a layman, coming in and recognising what has happened, should give him both to eat and to drink the things which the other forbade, he would manifestly seem to have helped. And such matters, among the works of handicraft (τῶν χειρωνακτέων), are especially made objects of contempt by people, for the physician or layman who came in seems to them as if he had even raised up a dead man. Because of pains the patients often become pulseless and faint and are unable to make any movement whatever, and in the same way also because of the acuteness of the disease; but some suffer in their power not on account of these things but on account of an emptying of the vessels that has come about in whatever way, whether through an excretion evident to perception, or through dispersal, or even through starvation. These, then, need to take nourishment as quickly as possible; on the contrary, those who are weak through pain or through the acuteness of the disease sometimes require evacuation rather than repletion.

But to these the one who gives nourishment does some very great harm; whereas if one presses those who are weak through emptiness of the vessels with a thin diet, [612] he would harm them, but not in a similarly conspicuous or acute way; yet it is more disgraceful to fail to recognise those who are weak through evacuation than those who are weak through pain. The rest of the passage is clear. Signs, then, will be written also concerning these matters, by which one must distinguish each of them. Here too, then, he again promises, as a little earlier, to write another book on acute diseases. These things, however, are also similar to those concerning the belly. For indeed, if the whole body rests much contrary to its habit, it is not immediately stronger; and if, having been idle for a longer time, it should suddenly come to exertions, it would manifestly fare somewhat badly. And so too each single part of the body.

B.translation: All these, then, are the injuries to the faculty that come about through evident causes; but there are others that are non-evident, as when, without evident evacuation or sleeplessness or starvation, or even the sensation in the mouth of the stomach, the patients are drawn down into such a condition of the body as he himself wrote of at the beginning of the Prognostic, saying: 'nose sharp, eyes hollow, [608] temples fallen in', and whatever follows these. For this state of the body comes about both through sleeplessness and through some copious excretion and starvation; but it comes about also without these, when the humours in the body happen to be thin and the heat of the fever acrid; for those that are thus thinned are dissipated imperceptibly. In some, too, the faculty becomes weak through the dyscrasia of one of the principles, when it is affected; first, then, the one primarily affected is distressed, and by sympathy the remaining two as well. For you have learned that there is one faculty in the nerves, having the brain as its principle; another in the arteries, whose principle is the heart; and a third in the veins, setting out from the liver. Sometimes, at any rate, a dyscrasia of any one of the parts whatsoever has damaged its own faculty, with which the remaining two faculties have been affected in sympathy. The swiftest deaths, then, occur when the heart is affected, next when the brain is, while those from the liver are slow.

For just as these parts [609], when affected by dyscrasia, suffer the greatest harm, each in its own faculty, so some parts lying near each of the principles, when they fall severely ill through dyscrasia, draw the principles of the faculties into sympathy with themselves; and some, even if they do not lie nearby, harm the parts that contain the principles of the faculties, through their community in kind or through some peculiarity of condition. Now the mouth of the stomach, when it draws the vital faculty into sympathy, brings on syncopes; when it draws the faculty specifically called psychic, deliria or convulsions; the uterus, again, brings on sometimes apnoeas, sometimes tensions of the nerves. But each of these, once fully developed, is plainly recognizable; while they are forming and increasing little by little, however, they escape the notice of most physicians. One ought not to recognize them only when they have become beyond help because of their magnitude, in the same way as laymen do, but while they are beginning and coming into being, for this is best; and if not that, then at any rate while they are increasing.

All such things, then, Hippocrates seems to me to have indicated through this phrase, in which he says: 'and all the affections and forms of every kind that our nature and condition engender in each of us' [610]; and here he calls 'nature' the mixture (krasis), and 'condition' (hexis) the constitution of the body itself. For those who are by nature of looser texture are dissipated and fall into syncope easily, while those of denser texture are protracted in their diseases. So too some people have certain parts colder and others hotter, some drier and others moister; and in all of them the disease is proper to the mixture. For it is a greater evil if, to a patient who is weak because of the pain and the acuteness of the disease, one administers more drink or gruel or food, supposing that he is weak because of emptiness of the vessels. But it is also shameful not to recognize a patient who is weak because of emptiness of the vessels, and to press him hard with the regimen. For this error too carries some danger, though much less than the other; yet this error is far more ridiculous than the other.

For if [611] another physician, or even a layman, comes in and, having recognised what has happened, gives the patient both to eat and to drink the things the other forbade, he would seem to have been manifestly of benefit. And it is above all such things on the part of practitioners of the craft that are held up to scorn by people; for the physician or layman who came in seems to them as though he had even raised up a dead man. On account of pains, patients often become pulseless and fall into fainting, and are unable to make any movement at all; and in the same way also on account of the acuteness of the disease. But some are afflicted in their strength not for these reasons, but through an emptying of the vessels that has come about in whatever way, whether through an excretion evident to perception, or through dispersal, or else through starvation. These, then, need to take nourishment as quickly as possible; but, on the contrary, those affected through pain or through the acuteness of the disease sometimes require evacuation rather than filling.

But for these, whoever gives nourishment does some very great harm; whereas those who are weak through emptiness of the vessels, if he presses them with a thin diet, [612] he would harm, though not in a similarly conspicuous or rapid way. It is, however, unseemly to fail to recognise that patients are weak through evacuation rather than through pain. The rest of the passage is clear. Signs will therefore be written about these things too, by which one must distinguish each of them. So here again, as a little before, he announces that he will write another book on acute diseases. These things, however, are similar to those concerning the belly. For if the whole body rests much beyond its habit, it is not at once the stronger; and if indeed, having been idle for a longer time, it suddenly comes to exertions, it would plainly fare badly. So too each single part of the body.
